sources.headline: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 76 held hostage for 17 hours
sources.text: De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly". He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.De la Espriella said the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused. Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women. But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre. Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked."We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police."He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied. "We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience."Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.Velázquez said the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives. He said that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above. Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers. Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded. The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces. A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage. Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.

sources.headline: Colombian police storm supermarket, freeing hostages and killing gunman
sources.text: Colombian police have stormed a supermarket and freed at least 20 people who were being held hostage, killing one of the gunmen.

sources.headline: Security forces storm scene, end Colombia supermarket siege
sources.text:
November 25, 2026 / 5:36 AM EST
/ CBS/AFP
Add CBS News on Google
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held hostage had been rescued and one captor killed. Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to have been held by armed men. "In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a video posted on social media.
A Colombian Army soldier is seen in the Exito Supermarket after security forces stormed the building to free hostages held by gunmen in Cartagena, Colombia, in the early hours of Nov. 25, 2026.
AFP via Getty Images
Shortly after midnight, a police helicopter hovered low over the shopping center as security forces massed outside the supermarket, AFP reporters saw. Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in. Ten of the roughly 30 people initially held had been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women. Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Exito supermarket as security forces secured the building.
De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and a sidearm while brandishing a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a roaring success. "We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively," he said, lauding the operation as "absolutely flawless." The president said one hostage-taker had been killed. Cartagena's mayor said all the hostages were "safe and sound" and would reunite with their families before undergoing medical checks.
Hostage takers were "caught off guard"The siege gripped Cartagena, one of Colombia's main tourist draws — a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship visits.Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside. "My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told AFP earlier in the standoff. "He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said. Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared on social media appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear carrying long guns alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.
Police officers at the entrance to a supermarket where a hostage-taking incident was in progress in Colombia's northern city of Cartagena on Nov. 24, 2026.
Xinhua via Getty Images
De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping -- no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said. Authorities said the siege began after an attempted armored vehicle robbery at the shopping center.
According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly $2 million, two armored vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles northeast of Cartagena. AFP couldn't independently verify those reports.The Rafael Nunez airport in Cartagena resumed landings after a brief suspension of about 45 minutes so the armed forces could use one of its runways in connection with the incident. the Reuters news agency reported.The siege unfolded on the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas and a series of attacks across the country. Despite the deal that ended the region's largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organizations still fight for control of parts of the country. Late Monday, authorities blamed a dissident FARC faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage. Separately, the presidency said a "terrorist attack" on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several southwestern departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

sources.headline: Twenty-five hostages taken in botched robbery in Colombia’s Cartagena
sources.text: CARTAGENA, Colombia - Gunmen held 25 people hostage in a supermarket in the Colombian tourist city of Cartagena on Nov 24, prompting a major police operation that saw snipers deployed around the building and nearby streets sealed off.The attackers appeared to have tried to rob an armoured vehicle before fleeing into the supermarket when police responded, taking about 30 people hostage, authorities said.Five hostages have since been released, all elderly women, President Abelardo de la Espriella said.The standoff unfolded in Cartagena, a Caribbean port known for its colonial old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism.Authorities briefly suspended arriving flights as security forces responded before later restoring operations.Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared widely on social media showed masked gunmen armed with rifles standing beside hostages who appeared to be kneeling on the floor inside the store.Police snipers took up positions on nearby buildings overlooking the supermarket.Several other officers crouched, weapons drawn at the entrance to the Exito supermarket, as the siege stretched into the afternoon.Scores of people gathered behind police cordons to watch the crisis unfold.Onlookers lined nearby roads and sidewalks, many filming on mobile phones as traffic was diverted around the shopping centre.Supermarket employees were among those feared taken captive.“My son is there,” Jacob Perez, father of one of the workers, told AFP. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said.Authorities have not identified the hostage-takers or said whether they belong to an organised criminal group.Local media reported the gunmen were demanding nearly US$2 million (S$2.5 million), two armoured vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, 130km to the north-east on Colombia’s Caribbean coast.AFP could not independently verify those reports.A police officer helping a woman during a reported hostage situation outside an Exito supermarket, in Cartagena, Colombia, on Nov 24. PHOTO: REUTERSThe hostage crisis comes on the 10th anniversary of the peace accord that led to the disarmament of the FARC guerrilla movement and amid a worsening security situation across parts of Colombia.Late on Nov 23, authorities blamed a dissident FARC faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.The right-wing De la Espriella has championed a hardline campaign against criminal groups, but violence has continued to rise in several parts of the country in recent months. AFP
